messages.body_plain:
Hi Shyam,
  This looks to me like a bug in the sna::prestige function when used 
with the degree-related versions of prestige.  It passes the nodes 
argument on to  degree() which returns a vector of the length nodes, 
which it then tries to subset using nodes -- which will contain out-of 
range indices that produce the NA.  As a work around, you can just 
subset the vector returned by prestige().  So if you want the value for 
vertex id 2

sna::prestige(faux.magnolia.high, gmode = "graph")[2]


but the calculations will be done using the full graph

best,
  -skye

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] [Help] Model and interpret edgecov results
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am very new to ERG modelling and I would like to clarify some confusions.

I am trying to understand how giving security advice and security
troubleshoot would affect security influence. For this purpose, I have
three binary networks: "give security advice", "give security
troubleshoot", and "influence security". The last one asked the participant
to nominate those who can influence their security behaviours.

My model is as followed:
inflNet ~ ostar(1) + edgecov(giveSecAdvice) + edgecov(giveTroubleshoot)

I believe ostar(1) means an out-directed tie which represents security
influence of one node to another. Each of the edgecov terms indicates the
existence of its respective tie in any directions.

My results are as followed:

                         Estimate Std. Error MCMC %  p-value

ostar1                                     -7.47033    0.38651      0
   < 1e-04 ***
edgecov.giveSecAdvice         3.04909     0.22970      1          < 1e-04
***
edgecov.giveTroubleshoot     2.55972     0.23052      1           < 1e-04
***
AIC: 3165    BIC: 3263

I have two questions:

1) Is it correct to interpret these results as: the conditional log odds of
the co-occurrence of a security influence tie, a give security advice tie,
and a give security troubleshoot tie is (-7.5 + 3.05 + 2.56), which is a
probability of 13.12%?

2) How should I model my ERGM (or what terms should I use) to determine
whether people who send out security advice and troubleshoot would be those
who influence other people as well? (i.e. entrainment effect of directed
ties coming from the same source)

Thank you.

Duy

messages.body_plain:
On Sun, 10 Jan 2016, Duy Pham Thien Dang wrote:


> I believe?ostar(1) means an out-directed tie which represents security influence of one node to another.

In a directed network, ostar(1) = edges, it's a baseline density term.  So 
here it would represent the baseline odds of nominating someone as 
influential.

> Each of the?edgecov?terms indicates the existence of its respective tie 
> in any directions.

No -- edgecov respects directionality (dyadcov is symmetric).  So in your 
case a positive coefficient would mean the direction is the same for both 
ties (e.g., nominate someone as influential that you giveSecAdvice to)

> My results are as followed:
>             ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ?Estimate Std. Error MCMC % ?p-value 
> 
> ostar1 ? ? ? ?            -7.47033 ?  ?0.38651 ? ? ?0 ? ? ? ? ?< 1e-04***
> edgecov.giveSecAdvice ? ?  3.04909 ? ? 0.22970 ? ? ?1 ? ? ? ? ?< 1e-04***
> edgecov.giveTroubleshoot ? 2.55972 ? ? 0.23052 ? ? ?1 ? ? ? ?  < 1e-04***
> AIC: 3165 ? ?BIC: 3263
> 
> I have two questions:
> 
> 1) Is it correct to interpret these results as: the conditional log odds of the co-occurrence of a security influence
> tie, a give security advice tie, and a give security troubleshoot tie is (-7.5 + 3.05 + 2.56), which is a probability of
> 13.12%?

Maybe a better way to think about it is

the logit of nominating someone as influential, without giving
Security advice or troubleshooting is -7.5 (p = 0.1%)

if you give security advice, it's -7.5+3.0 = -3.5 (p = 1%)

and if you also give troubleshooting it's -7.5+3.0+2.6 = -1.9 (p=13%). 
so, 130x more likely than the baseline probability.

> 2) How should I model my ERGM (or what terms should I use) to determine whether people who send out security advice and
> troubleshoot would be those who influence other people as well? (i.e. entrainment effect of directed ties coming from the
> same source)

So, for example, you want to know if i -> j as influential, whether j -> i 
as someone s/he gives secAdvice to?

If so, and your secAdvice matrix is set up as outgoing advice (row -> 
col), then if you transpose that matrix, it'll represent incoming advice, 
and you can use that as your edgecov.

> Thank you.
> 
> Duy
> 
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi

I have been trying out the ergm package the past day or so. I am exploring knowledge sharing networks and how these relate to innovation.

I have the following complete directed networks (constructed from a binary adjacency matrix):

- knowledge.provider.net
- affect.based.trust.net
- cognition.based.trust
- idea.generation.net
- idea.realisation.net

I postulate that trust is key to knowledge sharing, idea generation and idea implementation. Furthermore, I believe idea generation and idea implementation require knowledge sharing. To test for this I run the following models:

model.01 <- ergm(knowledge.provider.net~edges+
                mutual+
                edgecov(affect.based.trust.net)+
                edgecov(cognition.based.trust.net))

model.02 <- ergm(idea.generation.net~edges+
                mutual+
                edgecov(knowledge.provider.net)+
                edgecov(affect.based.trust.net)+
                edgecov(cognition.based.trust.net))

model.03 <- ergm(idea.realisation.net~edges+
                mutual+
                edgecov(idea.generation.net)+
                edgecov(knowledge.provider.net)+
                edgecov(affect.based.trust.net)+
                edgecov(cognition.based.trust.net))

All three models converge and seem to confirm my postulated hypotheses. There are significant covariate effects (which one can sort of see by examining plotted network graphs).  However, when checking goodness of fit, things start to unravel:

model.01.gof <- gof(model.01~ idegree + odegree + espartners + distance, directed = TRUE)

Some of my p-values are pretty low. So my questions to the list are: did I specify my ergm correctly and what adjustments could I try to improve my goodness of fit?

Thanks.


--

messages.body_plain:
Duy,

Have you examined the idegree distribution to see if there are any strange 
patterns in it?  You can do that with the summary command.  For example:

summary(net ~ idegree(1:20))

Or you can use the graphics from the gof command for the idegree 
distribution.

In principle, you should conduct exploratory analysis on all of the terms 
in your model -- the same way you would look at the univariate (and 
possibly bivariate) distributions for the covariates in a non-network 
setting.  You want to make sure there are no strange artifacts, inadequate 
cell counts, or just plain errors in the data.  The only difference here 
is that your covariates have to be constructed before you can conduct EDA 
on them.

In your previous email, you sequentially fixed the decay parameters in the 
gw* terms, but the values you chose did not match the values that were 
estimated when they were not fixed.  How did you choose the fixed values?

Finally, if controlling for idegree(7) changes your gw*sp terms to 
insignificant, this means the two are correlated, just as in a standard 
regression context.  There is no single "correct" way to handle this. 
Some might argue that degree terms establish basic constraints for all the 
other terms, and that interpretation is therefore cleaner when you control 
properly for the degree distribution before testing for higher order 
effects (like shared partners).  But Granovetter's classic article on the 
"The Theory Gap in Social Network Analysis" (1979) argued that this may 
not be the right approach, if e.g., the propensity to close triads is 
driving the degree distribution.

hth,
mm

messages.body_plain:
Dear Prof Morris,

Thank you for your reply.

Regarding the alpha and decay parameters in my two previous models:
Model 1:
inflNet ~ edges + gwdsp(0.2, fixed = TRUE) + gwesp(0.2, fixed = TRUE) +
gwidegree(1) + gwodegree(1)

Model 2:
inflNet ~ edges + gwdsp(0.2) + gwesp(0.2) + gwidegree(2, fixed = TRUE) +
gwodegree(2, fixed = TRUE)

I didn't follow any systematic approaches to select them and I just wanted
to experiment what would happen when fixing one set of parameters while
relaxing the other set.

By changing the decay parameters from 1 to 2, I also wanted to see the
effect caused by this change. As the model still converged and I received
similar significant results with negative signs, I (perhaps wrongly)
assumed that it didn't result in much difference.

---

At the moment, I fix all parameters at 0.1 and progressively increase them
until the model fails to converge. The max value of these parameters before
they make the model fail to converge appear to be 1.5. Interestingly, I
found quite a number of studies chose to fix parameters instead of relaxing
them too. I found this approach works for me because:

1) When I relaxed the parameters, they often resulted in degeneracy and the
model failed to converge. This happened when I combined these structural
features with the node's attributes in the models, and especially when the
alpha parameters of the gw*sp terms are relaxed.
2) Fixing all parameters increased significantly converge time.
3) I haven't clearly understood how to interpret the separate results of
the terms and their parameters when they are relaxed (as described in my
Question 1 in the other post), so fixing them gives me easier
interpretations.

Best regards,
Duy

messages.subject: [statnet_help] There may be excessive correlation between model terms
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] There may be excessive correlation between model terms
messages.body_plain:
Hello Andrew --

My guess is that your network is relatively dense, yes?  Our group has 
traditionally worked with relatively sparse networks, and our tutorials 
all reflected that.  Recently, as more folks have been modeling denser 
networks with ERGMs, we've come to see the same issue you are 
mentioning. The reason can be seen by thinking through the logic of what 
GWESP represents when alpha is 0: it simplifies to the number of edges 
in at least one triangle.  For sparse networks you would generally only 
expect a few edges to be in triangles, and then when you see a lot more 
then there is something special going on, and sufficient information to 
estimate what it is.  But for a dense network, you might expect nearly 
every edge to be in at least one triangle; effectively, the edges term 
and the GWESP(alpha=0) term are collinear. You are using a higher value 
for alpha -- 0.5 -- but it may still be sufficiently low that the terms 
are nearly collinear rather than exactly so.

My advice is to increase the starting alpha, perhaps into the range of 1 
to 2.  It may be easier to fix it in order to improve convergence, and 
then once you know you're in a realm that is successful, only then let 
it vary. Keep trying, and let us know what happens.

All of this has shown us that GWESP is even more subtle and complex than 
we had already appreciated.  There is a lot more theoretical work to be 
done around its interpretation in different settings, and its 
relationship to network concepts beyond just transitivity. Contributions 
to that literature, from you or anyone else reading this - are highly 
welcome!

Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Steps to develop an ERG model
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Steps to develop an ERG model
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am confused about the steps to develop an ERG model.

I read the paper "An introduction to exponential random graph (p*) models
for social networks" by Robins et al. (2007), and they explained the five
steps to construct a model. It reads to me that one would start by
constructing a model with (possibly) many terms/configurations that reflect
the hypotheses (Step 3), and then reduce/constrain the parameters to
achieve a more parsimonious model (Step 4). By doing this way, I imagine
that only one final model should be reported in a study.

However, I found quite a number of ERGM studies which constructed multiple
models and compare them. Specifically, they constructed a baseline model
which only has the "edges" term, then a "Pure Attributes" model which
describes homophily effects, then a "Structural" model (which either adds
new structural terms to the previous model or serves a standalone model),
then finally a "Combined" model with all the terms. They seem to follow an
approach that builds up the model's complexity over time, rather than
reduce the model's complexity to the finest state.

I would like to understand more about the differences of these approaches
to construct an ERG model. Could you please advise and/or point me to the
main literature about constructing ERG models?

Thank you very much.

Best regards,
Duy

messages.body_plain:
Hi Duy,
intersiting point, perhaps the authors of the paper you refer to will 
give a better answer, but I try to make some guesses.
I'm new to ergm too, anyway I think that the way you propose your model 
results must be connected to your theoretical formulations, and it does 
not depend on ergm (or whatever model you use) itself.
For example you might want to put in evidence the presence of spurious 
relations, and derive theoretical relevance from that. Let's say that 
model 1 contains only individual attributes, some of which are 
significant; then you run model 2 adding structural terms, and you find 
that individual attributes are no longer significant or have a weaker 
effect; this means that structural mechanisms actually prevail on nodal 
properties. And this is different than showing directly model 2 results. 
If past researches underline the importance of individual variables, you 
are now able to show  that even if some individual charachteristics may 
be associated with tie formation (model 1), there are structural forces 
that are actually responsible for that (model 2). So, only if it is 
theoretically relevant, showing both models' results allows you to show 
which specific social mechanisms are taking place.
Hope that helps, but I'm very curious to read others' comments.
Best,
Andrea
